title: Seurat and Pointillism
objective: After this level you can explain how dots of pure color blend in the eye.
summary: Seurat built La Grande Jatte from tiny strokes of pure color that blend in the viewer's eye: pointillism, shaped by Chevreul's color theories.

cards.headline: Up close, it's confetti. Step back, and it's a Sunday afternoon.
cards.body: Georges Seurat spent about two years on one giant painting made of tiny touches of color. Walk up to it and the people dissolve into specks. Walk away and they come back. The mixing doesn't happen on the canvas. It happens in your eye.

cards.headline: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte
cards.body: Seurat painted it in 1884–86. Parisians spend a Sunday afternoon on the Grande Jatte, an island in the Seine: some stroll along the river, some picnic on the grass. The canvas is huge, about 2 by 3 meters, wider than most sofas are long. And every inch of it is built from tiny, separate strokes of pure color, too small to pick out when you take in the whole picture.

cards.headline: Mixing in the eye, not on the palette
cards.body: That's pointillism: small dots or strokes of color placed side by side, so that from a distance they blend together. Why not just mix the paint first? Remember Level 4: mix complements as paint and they cancel into brown. Seurat kept his colors pure and separate, and let your eye do the mixing. The result seems to shimmer.
cards.callout: Paint mixed on the palette gets duller. Colors mixed in the eye stay bright.

cards.fact: Seurat met Level 4's color scientist, Chevreul, in person.
cards.context: He met the chemist Michel-Eugène Chevreul, then about 100 years old, the man who showed in 1839 that colors side by side change how each other look. Seurat experimented with his theories. He called his own method chromo-luminarism. Everyone else settled on pointillism (it's also called divisionism).

mascot.line: Your eye is doing the mixing. Congratulations: you're Seurat's unpaid assistant.

questions.prompt: What does Seurat's A Sunday on La Grande Jatte show?

options.label: A crowded café at night in Arles
options.rationale: That's closer to Van Gogh's Night Café.

options.label: Women praying after a sermon
options.rationale: That's Gauguin's Vision of the Sermon.

options.label: Parisians relaxing on an island in the Seine
A starry sky over a sleeping village

questions.explanation: It shows Parisians strolling and picnicking on a Sunday afternoon on the Grande Jatte, an island in the Seine.

questions.prompt: Why did Seurat set pure colors side by side instead of mixing them first?

options.label: Mixed paint dried too slowly for him
options.rationale: Drying time isn't the reason given.

options.label: So they'd blend in the eye and stay bright
He couldn't afford a palette
options.rationale: Nothing suggests that; it was a method.

options.label: So the picture would look rough up close
options.rationale: The dots are there to blend from a distance.

questions.explanation: Mixed as paint, colors dull (complements even turn brown). Kept separate, they blend in the viewer's eye and shimmer.

questions.prompt: Which scientist from Level 4 did Seurat meet and learn from?

options.label: Isaac Newton
options.rationale: Newton made his color wheel in 1704, long before Seurat.

options.label: Roger Fry
options.rationale: Fry was the critic who named Post-Impressionism.

options.label: Émile Bernard
options.rationale: Bernard was the painter Cézanne wrote to.

questions.explanation: Seurat met Chevreul, then about 100, and experimented with his theories about colors placed side by side.
